Hayley: Hey Adam! How's work going?
Adam: It's alright. There's a position that opened up at work. Boris told Kristi and I to apply for this internal position.
Hayley: That's great news! You have to apply then. Why do you sound so glum?
Adam: I don't think I'm cut out for it. I think Kristi will be better suited than I am anyways. Besides, she shouldn't have any difficulties getting the job.
Hayley: Did you tell her about what happened? You should tell her. You'll feel better.
Adam: I decided to tell her about what happened yesterday.
Hayley: How did she react to it?
Adam: She took it well. She asked why I never mentioned it earlier.

Hayley: So, you're not going to apply for it? You ought to give it a go.
Adam: No, I don't think I am going to apply. I'm working on something else. I feel I should step up my game at work. I've been falling behind ever since our last assignment.
Hayley: What are you working on?
Adam: Kristi wanted to know what I was going to do as well. I didn't tell her. I won't be telling you either. Let's just say in a few more days, I will have made a lasting impression at the office. I'll be doing everyone around the office a great service!
Hayley: What do you mean by that, Adam? You're not going to do something ridiculous ... are you?
Adam: I don't think it's ridiculous. In fact, you ought to believe me when I say it's a sensible idea.

Hayley: I've heard you say that many times before, Adam. Each time you did, I wondered what you meant. Let's just say these ideas of yours usually don't end well.
Adam: I know, but Hayley, trust me. I'll have thought this idea through a few times before I put it in motion.
Hayley: If you say so.

When you report what other people ask or command, you often make some grammar changes.

When you want to report an order, you usually use the following verbs: tell - command - order - forbid - ask - warn.
You use the infinitive after the report verb.
Boris told Kristi and I to apply for it.
She asked me to talk to her about it later.
She asked why I never mentioned it earlier.
They wanted to know what I did.

Modals Expressing Necessity, Duty or Advice
You can use a variety of modals to talk about what is necessary, what someone is responsible for and to give advice.

Let's look at the modals must, have to, have got to, and should.

You use the modal must when we decide for ourselves what is necessary.
Example:
I must show them I can live up to their expectations.

You use have to and have got to before verbs that talk about necessity. Have got to is more casual. Have to implies that someone else imposed the necessity on you.
Example:
You have to buckle down Kristi, and get it done.
I've got to work systematically.

Should is a modal you can use to give advice and to talk about duty.
Example:
You should make sure you meet these deadlines. (advice)
You should take this responsibility seriously. (duty)

We use should and ought to to make a subjunctive prediction.
Example:
They should/ought to win the next round easily.
She shouldn't have any trouble with traffic.
She shouldn't have any difficulties getting the job.
You should tell her. You'll feel better.
You ought to give it a go as well.
